songs.title: Turnstile Calculus
lines: Turnstile clicks and the city goes sideways,
Shoelace snagged where the last little sign sways.
I scribble a route on the back of a timetable,
Three stops closed and the fourth one unreliable.
Platform to pavement, a pattern of gravel,
Syllables shuffle where the streetlights unravel.
I catch that last syllable, carry it over,
Short step. Hard stop. Look past the shoulder.
A cab in the drizzle, its meter still blinking,
Driver says nothing, but I know what he's thinking:
If every detour is a price you are paying,
Who owns the map when the numbers stop saying?
I open the notebook, one page has a crease,
A list of directions and one little peace—
Not peace like a slogan, a piece of a ticket,
A route through a station whose door somebody picked.
Quick with the pivot, I'm skipping the barriers,
Buses are late so the bicycles carry us.
Pedals and puddles, a rattling basket,
Question in rhythm; I'm daring to ask it.
Who said the shortcut is always the winner?
Who drew the circle and called it the center?
I found an old staircase beneath the closed market,
Its steps kept the tempo and left me a margin.
Breathe at the landing. The railing is cold.
A baker is opening; the windows are gold.
He asks where I'm going. I point past the river.
He hands me a pastry and says, "Take it, traveler."
A city is larger than any direction,
More than the marks in the route's intersection.
I cross with the morning, the street slowly waking,
No glorious entrance. Just real progress making.

songs.title: Forecast Employees Union
lines: The weather report resigned at exactly five,
Said, "I've been predicting storms just to feel alive."
The clouds held a meeting in an unused bank,
The wind brought a whistle and forgot whom to thank.
A drizzle filed papers, three pages of mist,
The fog took attendance on a waterlogged list.
A lightning bolt shouted, "We need better hours!"
The thunder replied, "And a budget for flowers!"
Nobody asked the sun to work a double shift,
Nobody gave the raindrops any kind of lift.
If the sky wants a holiday, then let it have a day—
We'll hang our little umbrellas and politely float away.
The forecast hired a rainbow for its public-facing desk,
Who answered every question with a color-coded guess.
The hail asked for promotion, called itself "advanced snow,"
The breeze wrote, "I object," and then declined to blow.
A weather vane went missing, so the compass took its place,
Turned west to face the ocean, then forgot it had a face.
The sea sent up a memo: "Please stop sending storms at noon."
The moon sent back a postcard: "I don't handle them till June."
Nobody asked the sun to work a double shift,
Nobody gave the raindrops any kind of lift.
If the sky wants a holiday, then let it have a day—
We'll hang our little umbrellas and politely float away.
Then a little seedling whispered from a crack beside the road,
"Could someone send some water? I've been carrying this load."
The arguing went quiet and the clouds began to part;
The thunder cleared its throat as though embarrassed by its heart.
A single gentle shower fell for twenty minutes flat,
The seedling raised two leaves and never asked them more than that.
The forecast got promoted to a schedule with a choice:
"Occasional compassion" in a very official voice.
Nobody asked the sun to work a double shift,
But the clouds came back by choice, and that made the whole thing lift.

songs.title: Folded Map, Unsent Letter
lines: I found a folded map behind a drawer of string,
Where summer used to promise I could learn most anything.
The ink had soaked the corners and the towns were out of date,
I traced a crooked highway till my finger reached the lake.
I remembered all the mornings I had circled in a pen,
The place I'd planned on visiting, the call I'd make by ten.
The phone was on the counter, an old address in view,
I hadn't crossed that distance, though I always meant to do.
Some roads become a question you can carry for a year,
Some names keep their shape even when the ink isn't clear.
I folded up the paper, left it waiting on the chair—
A map can mark a distance; it can't put a person there.
The next day brought a drizzle and a bus with little heat,
I stood beside the window as the fields began to meet.
A boy in the next row was counting every sign,
As though the road were spelling out a language made of time.
We crossed the old stone overpass, the town appeared below,
The houses wore familiar roofs beneath unfamiliar snow.
I bought a little postcard, found a table by the square,
And wrote a sentence honest enough to leave the silence there.
Some roads become a question you can carry for a year,
Some names keep their shape even when the ink isn't clear.
I stamped the card and posted it beside a grocery stand,
A small and ordinary thing I finally understood to plan.
No trumpet from the clouds, no sudden answer in reply,
Only pigeons in the station and a widening of sky.
I rode back in the evening with the map inside my coat,
And remembered how a journey starts before you buy a boat.
A week later, there was writing in a different slanted hand:
"I kept your little postcard; yes, of course, I understand."
Some roads become a question; some return with something new,
And one short line of handwriting can tell you what to do.

songs.title: Two Sides of the Bridge
lines: BRIDGE: Everybody uses me but nobody knows my name.
RIVER: Everybody blames me when the banks won't look the same.
BRIDGE: They measure out my cables, call the crossing engineering.
RIVER: They measure out my levels, call my rising interference.
BRIDGE: I hold a thousand footsteps where the morning workers go.
RIVER: I carried little fishing boats before you learned to grow.
BRIDGE: You twist around my pillars; that's a dangerous little dance.
RIVER: You block the path of driftwood. I still give it half a chance.
BRIDGE: I am not your enemy, I'm trying to connect.
RIVER: Then learn to watch the current and accord it some respect.
BRIDGE: A little extra clearance, a new drawing for the span.
RIVER: I can show you where the water writes an older kind of plan.
BRIDGE: The surveyors are arguing; they want the work complete.
RIVER: The fishermen are waiting with their lanterns and their feet.
BRIDGE: I thought my job was standing still no matter how you bend.
RIVER: Mine is moving, and I rarely know exactly where I'll end.
BRIDGE: Perhaps I can be flexible without forgetting what I hold.
RIVER: Perhaps I can be gentle when the mountain rain is cold.
BRIDGE: We'll build another channel on the eastern edge of town.
RIVER: We'll let the winter water have a place to settle down.
BRIDGE: The drawing looks expensive.
RIVER: So does losing the whole shore.
BRIDGE: The council says a year.
RIVER: What were all those summers for?
BRIDGE: I'll keep the crossing open while they finish on the side.
RIVER: I'll carry all the silt away and leave a slower tide.
BRIDGE: When they cut the ribbon, will they say we found a way?
RIVER: They'll probably thank the mayor; that's the nature of the day.
BRIDGE: Then let the kids come running, let the bicycles roll through.
RIVER: And let the boats keep drifting like they always learned to do.
BRIDGE: I need you moving underneath.
RIVER: I need your shadow in the sun.
BOTH: A crossing isn't finished when the building work is done.
BOTH: It's finished when two different ways of living act as one.

songs.title: Terminal Four
lines: Coffee in the terminal, the boards are turning blue,
A thousand different flight plans, every one of them feels new.
Your suitcase by the window, my coat upon a chair,
I don't know how to phrase the part that hangs between us there.
The speakers call the morning, the rain begins to clear,
We talk about the small things when the bigger things are near.
A cup is growing colder as the boarding line appears,
I finally tell you plainly, "I am glad you spent these years."
Carry the good days in the side pocket,
Keep what you've learned even when you change roads.
Some doors will close, but the heart needn't lock it,
Some things stay home in the things that you hold.
A child drops a paper plane, it skids across the floor,
You catch it with a laughing hand and send it back once more.
The screen has changed your gate number, the line is moving on,
I pull the strap of your old bag and notice that it's torn.
I tie a little knot beneath the handle where it frayed,
And smile at all the ordinary repairs that we have made.
No promise from a movie, no dramatic final scene,
Only one repaired small handle and a cup between the seats.
Carry the good days in the side pocket,
Keep what you've learned even when you change roads.
Some doors will close, but the heart needn't lock it,
Some things stay home in the things that you hold.
I watch the little aircraft become a fleck against the cloud,
The terminal fills up again with footsteps talking loud.
A cleaner moves the chairs back and the coffee shop reopens,
I leave a tip and fold the napkin, grateful for the moment.
Maybe at some other gate, on some entirely different day,
We'll sit across another table with new stories on the way.
Carry the good days in the side pocket,
And leave enough room for the ones still on the way.

songs.title: Backroom Workshop
lines: Inside the backroom workshop every tool had found a place,
Except a cracked old metronome with dust across its face.
The apprentice tried to fix it with a screw and borrowed wire,
But every second skipped as though the clock was growing tired.
The master shook his head and said, "That piece won't make the sale,"
Then pointed to the mountain of repaired things on the rail.
The apprentice set it humming with a rhythm out of phase,
And counted every missing beat like footsteps in a maze.
Tap, tap, missing one; start again and keep it kind,
Not every broken measure means the music fell behind.
Tap, tap, missing one; hear the workshop answer back,
The tools can keep a rhythm when the clock forgets the track.
A neighbor brought a fiddle whose last string had come undone,
A dancer brought a boot with only half a heel for one.
The master heard the racket and came out to see the fuss,
The apprentice gave each person one small part of the chorus.
The hammer hit the table, the fiddle held the note,
The dancer stamped a rhythm on the workshop's wooden floor.
The little crooked metronome kept dropping every fourth,
So everybody filled that silence with a different kind of force.
Tap, tap, missing one; start again and keep it kind,
Not every broken measure means the music fell behind.
Tap, tap, missing one; hear the workshop answer back,
The tools can keep a rhythm when the clock forgets the track.
The master took the cover off and tightened one loose spring,
The needle kept its cadence; then there wasn't room to sing.
He loosened it a fraction and the silence came back through,
The room broke into laughter when he smiled and said, "That'll do."
They opened up the workshop on a Saturday at noon,
With broken things and borrowed tools and everybody's tune.
Tap, tap, missing one; the old refrain is almost done—
A missing little heartbeat made a place for everyone.
